title: Your £100 Grew to £127… So Why Does It Buy Less? 😬🛒 #shorts
description:
Your £100 grew to £127… and buys less.

Put £100 in cash on 1 January 2010 and let it earn exactly Bank Rate, interest added daily and left in, and by the end of September 2026 it's £126.73 (about £127). For twelve years it earned almost nothing: Bank Rate was between 0.1% and 0.75% from 2010 to 2021, so the £100 was only about £105.50 by January 2022.

Meanwhile prices raced ahead: the Consumer Prices Index went from 87.8 in January 2010 to 144.1 in September 2026, so what cost £100 then costs about £164 now (£164.12). Your £127 buys what about £77 bought in 2010: roughly 23% of its buying power gone.

The twist: right now Bank Rate is 3.75% (held on 17 September 2026) and CPI inflation was 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, so cash at Bank Rate is beating prices, but only just. The next Bank Rate decision is on 5 November 2026.

Sources: Bank of England Bank Rate history https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/boeapps/database/Bank-Rate.asp · https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy/the-interest-rate-bank-rate · ONS CPI index (D7BT) https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/timeseries/d7bt/mm23 · ONS Consumer price inflation, September 2026 https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/bulletins/consumerpriceinflation/september2026

Have you kept cash since 2010, or moved it? Would you still keep it in cash? Comment 👇

Prices = CPI, January 2010 to September 2026. General education, not financial advice.
